History and Physical (Detailed)

Consult Summary:
32-year-old male plastic surgeon with 1.5–2-month history of recurrent, worsening, right-sided sensory and motor episodes concerning for transient ischaemic attacks; urgently referred to TIA clinic.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Recurrent episodes of right-hand pins-and-needles with transient arm and leg weakness.  
• Onset/Timeline: Began ≈6–8 weeks ago; initially once weekly to monthly, now occurring a couple of times per day. Individual episode duration variably described as “a few days” before full resolution (possible internal inconsistency—see Quality Checks).  
• Progression: Increasing frequency; patient reports episodes are “getting more regular.”  
• Character/Associated features during episodes:
  – Right-hand paraesthesia (“pins and needles”) and numbness.  
  – Subjective right arm weakness; difficulty holding a coffee cup.  
  – Subjective right leg weakness; colleague noted abnormal gait.  
  – Sensation of “something in throat” but no true dysphagia.  
  – No dysarthria, no visual disturbance, no persistent swallowing difficulty.  
• Between episodes: Asymptomatic, feels “perfectly fine.”  
• Other systemic symptoms: General fatigue, intermittent nausea, low motivation.  
• No headache, no speech disturbance, no seizure activity mentioned.

Past Medical History:
• No chronic medical conditions reported.  
• Prior screening blood work (cholesterol, glucose, blood pressure) reportedly normal.

Medications:
• Aspirin 75 mg once daily – self-initiated; dose/route/frequency documented.  
Allergies:
• Penicillin – reaction details not stated (penicillin allergy).

Social History:
• Occupation: Medical doctor (plastic surgery).  
• Living situation: Lives with wife.  
• Tobacco: Non-smoker.  
• Alcohol / recreational drugs: Not discussed.  

Family History:
• Father: Carotid endarterectomy performed to reduce stroke risk (implies carotid atherosclerotic disease / TIA).  
• No other cerebrovascular or neurological conditions reported.

Physical Examination:
(Not performed—remote video consultation with loss of video feed; no vitals or examination findings documented.)

Investigations:
• Historic tests (date unspecified): Cholesterol, fasting glucose/diabetes screen, blood pressure – all reportedly normal.  
• No imaging, labs, or ECG performed during this consult.

Assessment & Plan:

Issue 1: Recurrent focal neurological episodes – suspected transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs).
  • Plan:
    – Urgent referral to local TIA / stroke clinic; referral sent during consultation. Target review within 1–2 days (Thursday–Friday).  
    – Anticipated clinic work-up: carotid Doppler ultrasound, brain imaging (CT/MRI), additional vascular/haematologic studies.  
    – Provide patient with TIA clinic and PALS contact numbers; advised to phone this afternoon or tomorrow morning to confirm appointment.

Issue 2: Risk of progression to stroke.
  • Plan:
    – Clear safety-net advice: If symptoms recur and are prolonged/persistent, attend Emergency Department immediately.  
    – If any delay in clinic appointment or inability to attend, contact GP service for further guidance.

Issue 3: Self-medication with aspirin.
  • Plan:
    – Documented; risks/benefits not fully reviewed in consult. Recommend medication review at TIA clinic or with GP; consider continuation vs cessation based on specialist advice.

General Plan items:
• GP to follow up on clinic outcome once results available.  
• Patient encouraged to maintain symptom diary, noting onset, duration, associated factors.  
• No driving advice documented; consider counselling once diagnosis confirmed.

Quality checks:

Missing / Expected elements:
• No objective neurological examination or vital signs documented.  
• Medication reconciliation incomplete (only aspirin recorded).  
• No alcohol history, exercise, diet, or detailed cardiovascular risk assessment.  
• Reaction specifics for penicillin allergy absent.

Internal conflicts:
• Episode frequency/duration conflict: described as lasting “few days” yet currently happening “a couple of times a day.”

Transcript quality:
• Occasional audio dropouts; minor clarity issues but clinically adequate narrative.
